newsitem.title: MACAU: Macau gambling monopoly unveils $US half-bln yield.
newsitem.headline: Macau gambling monopoly unveils $US half-bln yield.

text.p: Lifting a veil on 35 years' secrecy, Macau's gambling monopoly revealed on Thursday for the first time how much money it makes, reporting net profit of 4.63 billion patacas (US$579 million) for 1996.
Sociedade de Turismo e Diversoes de Macau (STDM) has held a casino monopoly in the Portuguese-administered territory, the south China region's gambling mecca, since 1962.
It presently operates nine casinos, and subsidiaries run the jockey club, a greyhound racetrack and several lotteries.
The company's annual report, published in Macau newspapers on Thursday under new laws for public franchises, showed gross income from gaming fell six percent last year.
Income from one-off, extraordinary items however resulted in seven percent growth for the final results, said the group which runs a number of enterprises including shipping.
"1996 was not very pleasant for the economy of the region of which Macau is part," the report said.
"We hope that 1997 and the following years will be more promising so that it will be possible to provide the Macau population with new jobs and social well-being," it added.
An economic downturn has hit Macau, sparking off a vicious gang war that has taken numerous lives as "triad" criminals fight for control over loansharking and protection rackets.
The violence is said to have scared off some tourists coming to Macau to gamble, particularly from nearby Hong Kong, just 40 km (25 miles) away, where gambling is under strict limits.

Gambling is the pillar of Macau's economy, and STDM has a monopoly lasting until the end of 2001, beyond the territory's 1999 reversion to China following four and a half centuries of Portuguese rule.

Government statistics show tourism and gaming generated 43 percent of Macau's gross domestic product in 1996, and STDM executives say over three-quarters of last-year's 8.1 million visitors to the territory came primarily for the gambling.

STDM pays nearly 32 percent of its gross takings as franchise taxes to the government, which has said casino takings in 1996 exceeded 16 billion patacas. It is estimated to provide as much as half of the government's current income.
